Those were the days, when we knew what we are not. When we knew 
that as between courts and agencies, Congress would usually think 
agencies the better choice to resolve the ambiguities and fill the gaps in 
regulatory statutes. Because agencies are “experts in the field.” And 
because they are part of a pohtical branch, with a claim to making 
interstitial pohcy. And because Congress has charged them, not us, with 
administering the statutes containing the open questions. At its core, 
Chevron is about respecting that allocation of responsibility—^the conferral 
of primary authority over regulatory matters to agencies, not courts.
Today, the majority does not respect that judgment. * * *
No t e s
1. 
The Court's Consideration of the Loper Bright and Relentless Cases. 
All nine Justices joined one of the opinions, even though Justice Jackson 
technically did not participate in the consideration of the Loper Bright case. 
The Court granted a companion case. Relentless v. Department of Commerce, 
decided by the First Circuit—^likely because Justice Jackson was recused from 
considering the D.C. Circuit’s decision in Loper Bright. The two cases were 
argued together, with Justice Jackson joining Justice Kagan’s dissent “only as 
it apphes” to Relentless. The facts and procedural posture of Relentless have 
been removed from the excerpt above, but they made no difference to the 
Court’s reasoning or disposition of the two materially identical cases.
2. 
The Source of the Standard of Review—Article HI'? Although the 
Court began its analysis by discussing the relationship between the standard 
of review for legal questions and the authority that Article III confers on courts 
to adjudicate “cases” and “controversies,” Loper Bright ultimately does not rest 
its holding on constitutional grounds. Instead, Chief Justice Roberts appeared 
to discuss Chief Justice Marshall’s famous statement from Marbury v. 
Madison—that “[i]t is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial 
department to say what the law is”—^to establish that de novo review of legal 
questions was the default rule during the pre-APA era. According to the 
majority. Congress adopted the APA against, and thereby incorporated, this 
default backdrop. By contrast, as Justice Thomas made clear in his separate 
concurrence, he would have declared the practice of Chevron deference 
rmconstitutional, because Article III requires de novo review. In turn. Justice 
Kagan disputed in her dissent that Marbury's de novo rule was the default 
approach by the time of the APA’s adoption.
The Court’s discussion of Article III raises three related questions. First, 
why did the Court elect not to rely on constitutional arguments against 
Chevron deference? Although any answer to that question is necessarily 
speculative, recall that judicial review of agency action traditionally occurred 
through a prerogative writ, such as mandamus, which seemingly carried a 
deferential standard of review. Had the Court embraced the argument that 
deferential review is always imconstitutional, it would have been forced to 
grapple with the constitutionahty of deferential review in the mandamus cases
